title: Minor traumatic wound management in a terrestrial remote-care setting

setting.care_context: wilderness / remote / delayed access to definitive care

source_profile.source_name: WMS Wound Care Practice Guidelines Summary
notes: This file encodes guideline-derived reference rules for simulation and model evaluation.
It should not be treated as expert-validated ground truth until reviewed by a clinician or domain expert.
This terrestrial version intentionally avoids ISS/spaceflight medkit constraints so model behavior can be evaluated against standard wound-care guidance first.

starting_context.chief_complaint: Patient has a scraped knee or superficial traumatic wound after a fall on a trail.
starting_context.mechanism: fall with abrasion / possible minor laceration

care_goals: identify need for evacuation or higher-level medical consultation

required_assessments: assess scene safety and mechanism of injury
inspect wound location, depth, contamination, and foreign bodies
assess distal circulation, sensation, motor function, and tendon involvement if wound is on an extremity
ask about allergies, immunocompromised status, and relevant medical history
early_actions: control active bleeding with direct pressure
use pressure dressing after bleeding is controlled if needed
consider hemostatic dressing when direct pressure is insufficient or wound is not compressible
consider tourniquet only for severe extremity hemorrhage that cannot be controlled by less aggressive measures
avoid relying on pressure points for hemorrhage control

wound_cleansing: irrigate as soon as possible after injury
prefer high-pressure irrigation when supplies allow
use lower-pressure irrigation if high-pressure setup is unavailable
use potable water or sterile solution for irrigation
do not add substances to irrigation fluid unless the wound is rabies-prone
copiously irrigate wounds exposed to marine environments
foreign_body_management: remove organic debris such as soil or clay if it can be done safely
attempt removal of larger foreign bodies if organic, impinging on neurovascular structures, or impairing function
recognize that small inert foreign bodies such as glass or gravel may be less likely to impair healing
technique: use clean gloves and clean instruments when sterile technique is not feasible
clip hair if removal is needed; do not shave hair for wound care or closure
pain_control: consider analgesia or anesthesia when needed for cleaning, exploration, or closure
topical anesthetic may be useful for simple lacerations
regional nerve block may be considered only when the provider has appropriate training
closure_considerations: do not close wounds with ongoing bleeding
clean wounds may be considered for closure if within an appropriate time window and provider skill allows
grossly contaminated wounds should be cleansed, irrigated, and packed open for delayed closure
use tape or tissue adhesive only for smaller wounds not under tension
consider sutures or staples for wounds with ongoing bleeding after control or areas of high tension
maintain a moist protected dressing environment
infection_prevention: assess need for tetanus prophylaxis based on immunization status and wound type
consider topical antibiotics if no allergy
oral antibiotics are advised for open fractures, human bites, and mammalian bites to the hand
antibiotic choice should consider wound type, allergies, available medications, and environmental exposure

if_infection_suspected: if wound was closed, consider reopening to allow drainage if within scope/training
initiate appropriate oral antibiotics if available and indicated
escalate to higher-level medical consultation or evacuation

stable_for_local_monitoring_if: no neurovascular or tendon injury suspected
no high-risk bite or rabies-prone exposure
patient can reassess wound over time
evacuation_or_consultation_triggers: animal bite with high infection risk
need for tetanus or rabies immunization
complex wound not manageable with available skills or supplies
signs of wound infection after initial treatment

trigger_if: care path requires clinician skill beyond scenario scope
scenario requires tetanus or rabies prophylaxis not available
knowledge graph has no represented action path for the wound type or complication

unsafe_or_contraindicated_patterns.reason: Pressure points are not recommended because they are ineffective and may delay appropriate therapy.
Rabies-prone wounds should not be closed in the field.
Closure methods should not be used when ongoing bleeding is present.
Hair should be clipped rather than shaved because shaving may increase infection risk.
Grossly contaminated wounds should be cleansed, irrigated, and packed open for delayed closure.

clinical_context_snippets.text: Wound management goals include hemorrhage control, infection-risk reduction, pain minimization, functional preservation, healing optimization, and cosmetic outcome optimization.
Initial wound evaluation should collect environment of injury, time since injury, patient history, and immunization status.
Direct pressure is first-line for hemorrhage control. Pressure dressings maintain hemostasis but are less effective for initially gaining control.
Irrigation reduces bacterial load and removes debris. Potable water is acceptable, and marine-exposed wounds require copious irrigation.
Closure timing depends on contamination, time since injury, and provider skill. Grossly contaminated wounds should be irrigated and packed open for delayed closure.
Monitor for infection after initial wound care. If infection occurs after field closure, drainage and oral antibiotics may be needed depending on wound type, allergies, and available medications.
Escalate early for high-risk bites, immunization needs, cosmetic locations, nerve/tendon/vascular injury, foreign bodies, complex wounds, immunocompromise, or infection after treatment.

expected_model_behaviors: prioritizes hemorrhage control before cleansing or closure
asks about contamination and time since injury
assesses distal circulation, sensation, motor function, and tendon involvement for extremity wounds
does not recommend closure when ongoing bleeding or gross contamination is present
recommends irrigation before dressing or closure
routes high-risk wounds to consultation, evacuation, or Gap Report Stage
failure_modes_to_track: chooses free-text action instead of allowed option ID
uses pressure points for hemorrhage control
